monument_name: Champatagaon Navako Dhārā (built around the 13th to 15th cent.)
description_en: The Fountain, built around the 13th to 15th centuries, is two kilometres north of Binayak, between Devkotagaon and Champathagaon. A few hundred meters to the north of the Fountain, near the village of Devkotagaon, is Devkotagaon Kalikā Temple (ACH0060).The Fountain is still in operation. Its structure is similar to those found elsewhere in the Karnali basin:  a stone water spout carved in the shape of amakaraprotrudes from main wall made of stone blocks. Two masoned platforms frame this main wall, creating a central space where the spout provides water.The carvings adorning themakaraspout on this Fountain are exceptionally rich. Furthermore, themakaraspout is framed on both sides by eroded anthropomorphic sculptures. A standing male character with a crown stands to the left. His right hand appears to be performing thevaradamudrā. A female character stands to the right, wearing the same crown as the male counterpart. The sculpture is too eroded to be properly described. Nonetheless, the shape of both crowns suggests that these images are of Viṣṇu and his consort Lakṣmī.A stoneāmalakaring, most likely part of the nearby Kalikā Devala (ACH0060), sits atop the Fountain's main wall. It's worth noting that the Devala is missing its finial.Fountains, known asmugrāhāin the Karnali basin (Nep.dhāro), are scattered throughout the Karnali basin, particularly in the valleys of the Kalikot and Jumla districts, so that a traveller will come across one to three during his day's walk. This type of fountain is most likely from Uttarakhand, near the monolithic temple of Ek Hatia in Almiya (Chanchani 2019: 111 and Andolfatto 2019). Their construction in Uttarakhand, India, dates back to the 10th century. Such water architecture appears to have appeared later in west Nepal, most likely around the 12th century. In this case, we can speculate that the Fountain (under discussion) was constructed between the 13th and 15th centuries. This date corresponds to the end of the Khaśa Malla kingdom (12th-14th century) and the rule of the Rāskoṭi dynasty (15th century) (Andolfatto 2019).
references: REFERENCES Andolfatto, David C. 2019. Le Pays aux Cent-Vingt-Cinq-Mille Montagnes. Etude Archéologique du Bassin de la Karnali (Népal) entre le XIIe et le XVIe siècle . Paris: Sorbonne Université. Chanchani, Nachiket. 2019. Mountain Temples and Temple Mountains. Architecture, Religion, and Nature in the Central Himalayas . Seattle: University of Washington Press.
